title: Mixing paints: how three colours make many more

summary.text: Mix yellow paint with blue paint, and you get green, a colour that was in neither pot. Your child mixes red, yellow and blue paint and finds orange, green, purple and brown. All three together make a dark, muddy brown. That is because paint absorbs, or soaks up, some of the light that falls on it. More paints soak up more light, so less light comes back to our eyes.
summary.art: A girl's hand holding a paintbrush over a steel plate with three blobs of paint, red, yellow and blue, and a fresh green patch where the yellow and blue meet.

intro.hook: Here is yellow paint, and here is blue paint. There is no green paint. Can we make green anyway?
intro.text: Put a blob of yellow paint and a blob of blue paint on a plate. Ask your child what colour they will make when stirred together, and why. Then let them stir. A green appears that was in neither pot. Where did it come from? This unit finds out.
intro.art: Two blobs of paint, one yellow and one blue, on a white plate, with a child's finger about to swirl them together.

outcomes: By the end I can say which colour two paints make: yellow and blue make green, red and yellow make orange, and red and blue make purple.
By the end I can say that red, yellow and blue are called primary colours, and that many colours can be mixed from them.
By the end I can say that every mix of paints is darker than the paler paint, and that red, yellow and blue together make dark brown.
By the end I can say that once two paints are mixed, I cannot get the first colours back out.
By the end I can say that paint absorbs, or soaks up, some of the light, and sends the rest back to my eyes.
By the end I can find colours around me, and say why many flowers and birds are so brightly coloured.

terms.meaning: Red, yellow, blue and green are colours. We see colours with our eyes, when there is light.
terms.example: A ripe mango is yellow and orange. A curry leaf is green.
terms.art: A yellow mango, a green curry leaf, a red tomato and a blue plastic bucket in a row.

terms.meaning: To mix is to stir two or more things together, so they become one.
terms.example: Stir yellow paint and blue paint together, and you have mixed them. They make green.
terms.art: A paintbrush stirring a yellow blob and a blue blob into one green swirl on a steel plate.

terms.meaning: Red, yellow and blue are the primary colours of a paint box. You cannot mix them from the other paints in the box, but you can mix many other colours from them.
terms.example: Red and yellow make orange. Orange is not a primary colour, because you can mix it.
terms.art: Three round pots of paint, red, yellow and blue, with small arrows pointing to orange, green and purple patches below them.

terms.meaning: To absorb is to soak up. Paint absorbs some of the light that falls on it, and sends the rest back to our eyes.
terms.example: A towel absorbs water. Dark paint absorbs a lot of light, so it looks dark.
terms.art: A towel soaking up spilt water next to a dark brown paint patch with a torch beam shining on it and very little light bouncing off.

explanations.concept: Two paints make a new colour
explanations.definition: When you mix two paints, you get a new colour. Yellow and blue make green. Red and yellow make orange. Red and blue make purple.
explanations.description: In the Colour Mixing Test, you stirred yellow and blue paint together, and green came out, though neither pot was green. Red and yellow made orange, like a marigold. Red and blue made purple, like a brinjal. A lot of yellow and a little blue make a light green. A lot of blue and a little yellow make a dark green.
examples: Yellow and blue make green, the colour of a parrot or a banana leaf.
Red and yellow make orange, the colour of a marigold or a carrot.
Red and blue make purple, the colour of a brinjal or a jamun.
explanations.context: This card says what you found in the Colour Mixing Test, when you mixed two paints at a time.
explanations.art: Three colour sums painted on paper: a yellow blob plus a blue blob equals a green blob, red plus yellow equals orange, and red plus blue equals purple.

explanations.concept: Primary colours: the three you start with
explanations.definition: Red, yellow and blue are the primary colours of a paint box. You cannot mix them from the other paints in the box. Many other colours can be mixed from them.
explanations.description: Try to mix yellow from the other paints. Red and blue make purple, never yellow. So yellow has to come from its own pot, and so do red and blue. Primary means first.
examples: Orange, green and purple can all be mixed from red, yellow and blue.
explanations.context: This card is about the three paints you started with in the Colour Mixing Test.
explanations.art: A child's paint box with red, yellow and blue cakes, and beside it a colour printer's three ink cartridges in yellow, magenta and cyan.

explanations.concept: Why mixing paints makes colours darker
explanations.definition: Paint absorbs, or soaks up, some of the light that falls on it. It sends the rest back to our eyes, and that is the colour we see. Two paints together absorb more light than one, so a mix is darker.
explanations.description: Sunlight and lamp light are made of many colours mixed together. Yellow paint soaks up the blue part of the light and sends back the rest. Blue paint soaks up the red, orange and yellow parts. Together they soak up nearly everything except green, so green is the light left to reach your eyes. Add red paint too, and the green is soaked up as well. Very little light comes back, so you see dark brown.
examples: In the Colour Mixing Test, every mix was darker than yellow.
Red, yellow and blue together made a dark, muddy brown.
In a dark room, no light falls on the paint, so every colour looks black.
explanations.context: This card says why your mixes came out darker, and why all three paints made brown.
explanations.art: A simple drawing of a torch shining on a yellow paint patch, a blue paint patch and a green patch, with fewer and fewer little arrows of light bouncing back, and almost none from a brown patch.

explanations.concept: Colours around us, and colours on living beings
explanations.definition: Many colours come from colour stuff in paint, flowers and feathers. Some colours come from tiny shapes instead, like the shine on a pigeon's neck.
explanations.description: Flowers use bright colours to call bees and butterflies to their nectar. A pigeon's neck shines green and purple as they turn their head. Tiny layers in the feathers make those colours. A green parrot has yellow colour stuff in the feathers and tiny shapes that send back blue, so yellow and blue together look green, like your paints.
examples: A marigold's orange calls bees and butterflies.
A pigeon's neck changes from green to purple as they turn.
A green parrot's feathers are yellow and blue together.
explanations.context: This card is about the colours you found in the Colour Hunt and at the window.
explanations.art: A pigeon on a window ledge with a shining green and purple neck, a green parrot on a neem branch, and a bee landing on an orange marigold.

agreed.text: Mixing two paints makes a new colour.
agreed.evidence: Yellow and blue paint make green, red and yellow make orange, and red and blue make purple. Anyone with a paint box can try it.
Every mix is darker than the paler paint, and red, yellow and blue together make dark brown. Each paint absorbs some light, so a mix absorbs more.

agreed.text: We need light to see colours.
agreed.evidence: In a dark room, every paint looks black. Switch on a light, and the colours come back.

challenging.claim: Mixing all the colours together makes white.
challenging.who: A common guess among children, and many grown-ups
challenging.for: Sunlight is all the colours of the rainbow together, and it looks white. You will find this out in a later unit.
challenging.against: That is true for light, but not for paint. Mix all your paints, and you get dark brown, because every paint soaks up more light.
challenging.context: This card is about what happens when you mix every paint at once.

challenging.claim: Red, yellow and blue are the only true primary colours.
challenging.for: In a child's paint box, you cannot mix red, yellow or blue from the other paints.
challenging.against: Printers use yellow, magenta and cyan, and from these they can mix red and blue. For light, the primary colours are red, green and blue. Which three you start with depends on what you are mixing.
challenging.context: This card asks whether there is only one set of primary colours.

challenging.claim: You can always unmix a colour if you try hard enough.
challenging.for: Paint looks like it might come apart if you add more of one colour.
challenging.against: Adding more yellow to green makes a yellowish green, never plain yellow. Adding water makes a paler green. The two paints stay mixed.
challenging.context: This card is about trying to get yellow back out of green.

big_questions.q: Green was in neither the yellow pot nor the blue pot. So where did the green come from?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each paint does to light. What light is left over when both paints are there?

big_questions.q: If you mix a colour that no one has ever mixed before, have you invented it?
big_questions.hint: Could someone else mix the same colour? Was the colour waiting there all along?

big_questions.q: In the dark, is a red tomato still red?
big_questions.hint: What do you see in the dark? What does the tomato need, so that it can send red light back to you?

big_questions.q: A bee sees colours on a flower that you cannot see. Whose flower is the real flower, the bee's or yours?
big_questions.hint: Is one of you seeing it wrong? Or does each body meet the flower in its own way?

story.title: Lakshmi's Green Parrots
story.note: Srikalahasti in Andhra Pradesh is a real centre of Kalamkari, cloth painted by hand with a bamboo pen called a kalam, using colours from plants. Kalamkari painters make green by painting yellow over indigo blue. Green parrot feathers really do combine a yellow pigment with tiny structures that scatter blue light. Ammamma means mother's mother in Telugu. Lakshmi, Ammamma and Ravi are made up.
text: Lakshmi was six. She lived in Srikalahasti, a town in Andhra Pradesh. Her grandmother, Ammamma, painted pictures on long pieces of cotton cloth. This kind of painting is called Kalamkari.
Ammamma did not paint with a brush. She used a bamboo pen called a kalam, with a little ball of cloth tied near the tip to hold the colour.
That morning, Ammamma spread a big cloth on the floor of the verandah. She had drawn a big tree, full of birds.
"These are parrots," said Ammamma. "You may paint them, Lakshmi."

Lakshmi clapped. Then she looked at the pots of colour. There was a pot of dark blue, made from the leaves of the indigo plant. There was a pot of yellow, made from boiled pomegranate peel. There was a pot of red.
"Ammamma, where is the green?" asked Lakshmi. "Parrots are green."
"There is no green pot," said Ammamma. "Paint the parrots blue."
"Blue?" said Lakshmi. "But parrots are not blue!"
"Trust me," said Ammamma, and smiled.
So Lakshmi painted every parrot blue. Her cousin Ravi, who was eight, came out to look. He laughed. "Blue parrots! Whoever saw a blue parrot?"
The blue dried in the sun. Then Ammamma gave Lakshmi the yellow. "Now paint the yellow on top of the blue," she said.
Lakshmi painted carefully. Where the yellow went over the blue, something happened. The parrot turned green. Bright parrot green!
Lakshmi stared. "Where did the green come from? It was not in any pot."
"The yellow and the blue made it together," said Ammamma.

Lakshmi wanted to try more. Ammamma gave her a scrap of cloth to practise on. Lakshmi mixed a little red with the yellow. It turned orange, like a ripe mango. She mixed red with blue. It turned purple, like a jamun.
"If two colours make a new colour," said Lakshmi, "then three colours will make a super colour!"
She mixed red, yellow and blue all together. She stirred and stirred. But the super colour was not bright at all. It was dark and brown.
Ravi laughed again. "You made mud!"
Lakshmi's lip shook. She added more yellow, to make it bright again. It stayed brown. She added more yellow to the green, to get her yellow back. It turned yellowish green, but never plain yellow.
"Ammamma, I cannot get my colours back," she said.
Ammamma put an arm around her. "Once two colours have met, they stay together," she said. "And every colour you add makes the mix a little darker. But look. What colour is the trunk of this tree?"
Lakshmi looked at the tree on the cloth. It had no colour yet. Then she looked at her brown mix.
"Brown!" she said. And she painted the whole trunk with her mud.
Ravi stopped laughing. "Can you show me how to make orange?" he asked. So Lakshmi showed him, and he painted mangoes on the tree.
That evening, a real green parrot landed on the neem tree outside their house. She screeched and cracked a seed in her red beak.
Lakshmi whispered, "Did someone paint you yellow on blue?"

"Nobody painted her," said Ammamma. "But scientists have looked closely at parrot feathers. A green feather has yellow colour inside it. It also has tiny shapes that send back blue light. Together, they look green."
Lakshmi looked at the parrot, and then at her painted parrots. "So she is yellow and blue, just like mine," she said.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Lakshmi finds that green can be made from yellow and blue, that mixing all three makes a dark brown, and that mixed colours cannot be separated again. Then she sees that a real parrot's green is made of yellow and blue too.
ask: There was no green pot. How did Lakshmi make her parrots green?
Why did Lakshmi's super colour come out dark brown?
Could Lakshmi get her yellow back out of the green? What happened when she tried?
What colours are inside a real parrot's green feathers?
art: A grandmother in a cotton saree sitting on a verandah in Srikalahasti, drawing on a long cloth with a bamboo pen, while a girl of six watches.
Three clay pots of colour, dark blue, yellow and red, beside a cloth with a tree full of blue-painted parrots.
The girl painting yellow over a blue parrot, and the parrot turning bright green where the yellow goes.
A boy of eight laughing at a dark brown smudge on a scrap of cloth, and the girl looking upset.
The girl painting the tree's trunk brown while the boy paints orange mangoes on the branches.
A real green parrot with a red beak on a neem branch at dusk, with the girl and her grandmother looking up at her.

experiments.title: The Colour Mixing Test: what can three paints make?
experiments.context: In this experiment you mix red, yellow and blue paint, two at a time, and see what new colours come out. Then you mix all three. Then you try to get a colour back.
experiments.question: What colour will two paints make when you mix them? And what happens when you mix all three?
experiments.predict: Before each mix, guess the new colour. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same small blob of each paint, about the size of a green pea, for every mix. Wash the brush in water between mixes, so no old colour sneaks in.

materials.item: red, yellow and blue paint: poster colours, a watercolour box or finger paint
materials.buy: Poster colours are sold in any stationery shop. At home, food colours stirred into a little water work too.

materials.item: an old white plate or a steel plate, to mix on
a paintbrush, or cotton buds (earbuds)
a sheet of white paper
a tumbler of water and an old cloth
old newspaper to cover the floor or table

experiments.safety: Paint is not food. Keep it away from mouths, and wash hands after.

schedule.what: Guess and mix two paints at a time, mix all three, then try to get yellow back.

experiments.record: Paint your colour sums on the paper: a yellow blob, a plus sign, a blue blob, an equals sign, and the green you made. Do the same for every mix.

setup.art: A white plate on newspaper with three pea-sized blobs of paint far apart, red, yellow and blue, and a brush and tumbler of water beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Put three small blobs of paint on a plate, far apart.

setup.art: A child's brush pulling a little yellow and a little blue into the middle of the plate and stirring them into green.
setup.caption: 2. Mix two paints in the middle. What colour comes?

setup.art: A sheet of paper with painted colour sums: yellow plus blue equals green, red plus yellow equals orange, red plus blue equals purple.
setup.caption: 3. Paint each colour sum on paper.

flow.do: 1. Cover the table with newspaper. 2. Put a pea-sized blob of red, yellow and blue paint on the plate, far apart. 3. Put the water and cloth nearby.
flow.say: Here are three paints: red, yellow and blue. Today we will mix them, two at a time. What do you think yellow and blue will make? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the three paints. Red, yellow and blue. What will yellow and blue make? Why?

ask.q: What do you think yellow and blue will make? Why?

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Don't say what will happen. Write the guess in the table.

flow.do: 1. Your child takes a little yellow on the brush and puts it in the middle of the plate. 2. They wash the brush and add a little blue. 3. They stir. 4. They paint a patch of the new colour on the paper.
flow.say: Take a little yellow. Now wash your brush and take a little blue. Stir them together. What colour is coming?
flow.kid: Take yellow. Wash the brush. Take blue. Stir. What colour do you see?

good: Green, but neither pot was green.

flow.parent: Children are often surprised. Let them enjoy it before you ask where the green came from.

flow.do: 1. Guess, then mix red and yellow in a clean spot. 2. Guess, then mix red and blue. 3. Paint each new colour on the paper, with its colour sum.
flow.say: Now red and yellow. What will they make, and why? Let's mix. Now red and blue. What will they make?
flow.kid: Guess first. Then mix red and yellow. Then mix red and blue.

ask.q: What did red and yellow make? What did red and blue make?

flow.parent: Poster red often has a little yellow in it, so red and blue can come out a dull, brownish purple. A pink red gives a brighter purple. Both are real results.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess what all three paints will make together, and why. 2. They mix a little red, yellow and blue in one spot. 3. They paint it on the paper.
flow.say: What will all three make together? Why do you think so? Let's mix them. Is the new colour brighter or darker than the yellow?
flow.kid: Guess first. Then mix all three. Is it bright or dark?

ask.q: What did all three paints make?
good: A muddy colour, darker than all of them.

flow.parent: Many children expect a rainbow or a bright colour. A dark brown is the right result. Don't explain why yet. The explanation card comes after.

flow.do: 1. Your child takes some green from the plate and adds more and more yellow. 2. Look at the colour after each brushful.
flow.say: Can we get the yellow back out of the green? Add more yellow. Is it yellow again?
flow.kid: Add more yellow to the green. Is it yellow again?
flow.parent: The green turns yellowish green, but never plain yellow. Now ask: what did you find, and what did you see that shows it?

check.q: A girl mixes yellow and blue paint. Then she adds lots more yellow. What does she get?
check.why: Once two paints are mixed, they stay mixed. More yellow makes the green paler and more yellowish, but the blue is still there.

experiments.title: Drop by Drop: can water undo green?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make yellow water in a glass, then add blue one drop at a time. You watch the green get darker. Then you try to turn it back into yellow with water.
experiments.question: Each drop of blue makes the green darker. Can adding water turn the green back into yellow?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will lots of water make the green yellow again? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Stir the same number of times after every drop. Look at the glass against the same white paper each time.

materials.item: 2 clear glass tumblers or clear plastic cups: one half full of water, one empty
yellow and blue food colour, or a brush-tip of yellow and blue poster paint
a spoon to stir
a sheet of white paper to stand the glasses in front of
a jug of water

schedule.what: Make yellow water, add blue drop by drop, then try to undo the green with water.

experiments.record: Draw the glass after 1 drop, 3 drops and 6 drops of blue. Colour each drawing.

setup.art: A clear glass of yellow water standing in front of a white sheet of paper, with a dropper or a brush tip holding blue colour above it.
setup.caption: 1. Make yellow water. Add one drop of blue.

setup.art: Three glasses in a row, light green, green and dark green, with 1, 3 and 6 dots drawn under them.
setup.caption: 2. Add drops one at a time. Watch the green get darker.

setup.art: A child pouring water from a jug into a glass of green water, which turns paler green.
setup.caption: 3. Pour in lots of water. Is it yellow again?

flow.do: 1. Half fill a glass with water. 2. Add yellow food colour, a drop or two, and stir. 3. Stand the glass in front of the white paper.
flow.say: Here is yellow water. I will add one drop of blue. What colour will it turn? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the yellow water. Guess what one drop of blue will do.
flow.parent: If you use poster paint, dip the brush tip in blue and swirl it in the water. One swirl counts as one drop.

flow.do: 1. Your child adds one drop of blue and stirs. 2. They count each drop out loud, up to six. 3. Look at the colour after each one.
flow.say: Add one drop. Stir. What colour now? Add another drop. Is the green lighter or darker?
flow.kid: Add one drop. Stir. Count. Is it lighter or darker now?

ask.q: What happens as you add more blue?
good: It went from light green to dark green.

flow.do: 1. Pour half the green water into the empty glass. 2. Ask your child to guess. 3. They fill that glass to the top with plain water from the jug and stir. 4. Stand it beside the first glass to compare.
flow.say: Can water turn the green back into yellow? What do you think, and why? Let's pour in lots of water.
flow.kid: Pour in lots of water. Is it yellow again?

good: Lighter, but still green, not yellow.

flow.parent: Water spreads the colours out, so the green gets paler. But the yellow and blue are both still there, so it stays green.

flow.do: Stand the two glasses side by side and look at them together. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: So, did the water undo the green?
flow.kid: Did the water undo the green?

check.q: A girl pours lots of water into her green water. What colour does it turn?
check.why: Water spreads the yellow and the blue out, so the green gets paler. Both colours are still there, so it stays green.

activities.title: Colour Hunt: one thing of every colour
activities.context: This is a short noticing activity, before anyone explains anything. You hunt around your home for one thing of every colour and put them in heaps.

materials.item: 8 small paper slips and crayons
a white bedsheet or a clear patch of floor

schedule.what: Find one thing of each colour and put it by its slip.

activities.record: Draw the colour you found hardest, and the thing you found for it.

setup.art: Eight crayon-coloured paper slips laid in a row on a white bedsheet: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple, brown and black.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the colour slips.

setup.art: A girl putting a green curry leaf by the green slip, with a red tomato and a yellow lemon already by their slips.
setup.caption: 2. Find a thing for each colour, and put it by its slip.

flow.do: 1. Colour the eight paper slips with crayons: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple, brown and black. 2. Lay them in a row on the sheet.
flow.say: We are going on a colour hunt. Find one thing for each colour, and put it by its slip.
flow.kid: Find one thing for each colour. Put it by its slip.

flow.do: Your child hunts around the home and places each thing by its slip.
flow.say: Can you find something purple? Now something orange. Which colour is the hardest to find?
flow.kid: Find something purple. Now orange. Which is the hardest to find?

ask.q: Which colour was hardest to find? Why do you think so?
good: Purple, because there isn't much purple at home.
Blue was easy, because the bucket is blue.

flow.parent: Good finds: a tomato, a carrot or marigold, a lemon or turmeric, a curry leaf, a bucket, a brinjal or jamun, a wooden spoon, a pot or hair band. Purple is often hardest.

flow.do: Look at the heaps together, and ask the check question.
flow.say: Look at your green thing. Do you think we could make that green with paint?
flow.kid: Look at your green thing. Could we make that green with paint?

check.q: Which two paints could we mix to make the green of a curry leaf?
check.why: Yellow and blue make green. Red and blue make purple, and red and yellow make orange.

activities.title: Kitchen Paints: colours from turmeric and beetroot
activities.context: In this activity you make paint from things in the kitchen, the way people made colours long ago. Then you mix them.

materials.item: half a teaspoon of turmeric powder
a slice of beetroot
2 small steel bowls and a few spoons of water
a paintbrush or cotton bud
a sheet of white paper

schedule.what: Make yellow and pink paint, paint with them, then mix them.

activities.record: Paint a flower with your kitchen paints, and the colour you got when you mixed them.

setup.art: Two small steel bowls, one with bright yellow turmeric water and one with deep pink beetroot juice, beside a slice of beetroot.
setup.caption: 1. Make yellow paint and pink paint.

setup.art: A child painting a flower on paper with the yellow and pink kitchen paints, and an orange patch where they mixed.
setup.caption: 2. Paint, then mix the two.

flow.do: 1. Stir the turmeric into 2 spoons of water in one bowl. 2. Cut the beetroot and squeeze or press the slice into a spoon of water in the other bowl.
flow.say: Long ago, people made paints from plants. Let's make yellow from turmeric and pink from beetroot.
flow.kid: We are making paint from the kitchen. Yellow from turmeric. Pink from beetroot.
flow.parent: The beetroot juice comes out deep pink to red. If it is faint, rub the slice on the wet bowl. Turmeric makes a strong yellow, though it does not fully dissolve.

flow.do: Your child paints with each colour, then mixes a little of both in a spoon.
flow.say: Paint with the yellow, and then the pink. What will they make together? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Paint with yellow. Paint with pink. Guess what they make together.

ask.q: What did yellow and pink make?
good: A reddish orange, like a marigold.

flow.do: Talk about the colours, and ask the check question.
flow.say: These colours came from plants. Turmeric and beetroot come from plants that grow in the ground. What other plant colours do you know?
flow.kid: These colours came from plants. What other plant colours do you know?

check.q: Where did our yellow paint come from?
check.why: Turmeric is dug from the ground. The turmeric plant makes that yellow inside the part we dig up.

activities.title: Colour at the Window: flowers, leaves and birds
activities.context: In this activity you look closely at the colours of living beings: a potted plant, and a pigeon or crow at the window. You ask why they have those colours.

materials.item: a potted plant, or flowers and leaves from the kitchen, such as curry leaves or a marigold
a window where pigeons, crows or sparrows sometimes come

schedule.what: Look at a plant up close, then watch for a bird at the window.

activities.record: Draw a bird or a flower you saw, and colour the drawing in.

setup.art: A child kneeling by a potted hibiscus on a balcony, looking closely at a red flower and its green leaves.
setup.caption: 1. Look closely at a plant's colours.

setup.art: A pigeon on a window ledge turning their head, their neck shining green on one side and purple on the other.
setup.caption: 2. Watch a pigeon's neck as they turn.

flow.do: Look at the plant together. Count how many greens you can see on the leaves.
flow.say: How many different greens can you see on this plant? Why do you think a flower is so bright?
flow.kid: How many greens can you see? Why is the flower so bright?

ask.q: Why do you think the flower is so bright?

flow.parent: Flowers use bright colours to call bees and butterflies to their nectar. Bees see a kind of light called ultraviolet, which we cannot see, so a flower may look different to a bee.

flow.do: Watch the window for a pigeon or a crow. If none comes, try again later in the day. Any bird is fine.
flow.say: Look at the pigeon's neck. What colour is it? Now watch as they turn their head. Does the colour change?
flow.kid: Look at the pigeon's neck. Watch it as they turn.
flow.parent: A pigeon's neck shines green and purple, and the colours change as they move. Tiny layers in the feathers make these colours, not pigment. Pigeons come to most city windows.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Why do many flowers have bright colours?
flow.kid: Why are many flowers so bright?

check.q: Why do many flowers have bright colours?
check.why: Bright colours help bees and butterflies find a flower's nectar. As they visit, they carry pollen from flower to flower.

games.title: Colour Sums: say what they make
games.players: 2 or more players. A grown-up reads the cards.
games.context: This is a card game about mixing. Each card shows two colours. You say what colour they make, then turn the card over to check.

items.f: Lots of yellow + a little blue
Lots of blue + a little yellow

rules: Before you play, colour a small blob of each colour next to its word on the front of each card, so everyone can read the cards.
Put the cards in a pile, colour sum side up.
On your turn, look at the top card and say what colour the two make.
Turn the card over to check. If you were right, keep the card.
If you were wrong, say what the two colours make together and put the card aside. Nobody keeps it.
When the pile is empty, the player with the most cards wins. If you have the same number, play again.

setup.art: A card with a yellow crayon blob, a plus sign and a blue crayon blob, and its back showing a green blob and the word Green.
setup.caption: 1. Colour the blobs on each card.

setup.art: A mother holding up a card while a girl says 'Orange!' and points at an orange crayon.
setup.caption: 2. Say what the two colours make, then turn the card over.

flow.do: 1. Colour the blobs on the cards together. 2. Put them in a pile.
flow.say: Each card shows two colours. You say what they make together. Then we turn it over to check.
flow.kid: Look at the two colours. Say what they make.

flow.do: Take turns with the cards.
flow.say: Red and yellow. What do they make? Let's turn it over. Were you right?
flow.kid: Say what they make. Turn it over. Were you right?

good: We mixed it in the test.
Red and yellow made orange on the plate.

flow.parent: If your child is unsure, let them mix the two paints to find out. The paint is the real answer.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Which card was hardest? Why?
flow.kid: Which card was hardest?

check.q: A card says "Lots of yellow + a little blue". What does it make?
check.why: Lots of yellow makes the green lighter. Lots of blue would make it darker.

games.title: Mix and Run: hold up the colours, then find one
games.players: 2 or more players. One calls, and the others hold up cards and run.
games.context: This is a moving game. The caller says a mixed colour. You hold up the two primary colours that make it, then run to touch something of that colour.
rules: Print the page once for every two players. Each player takes three cards and colours them: one red, one yellow and one blue.
The caller says a mixed colour: green, orange or purple.
Each player holds up the two cards that make that colour.
Then everyone runs to touch something in the home of that colour. If you cannot find one, name something you know that has that colour.
Say what you touched. Then the caller says a new colour.
Take turns being the caller. Stop when everyone has called once.

setup.art: Three cards coloured red, yellow and blue with crayons, held in a child's hands.
setup.caption: 1. Colour one card red, one yellow and one blue.

setup.art: A girl holding up a yellow card and a blue card, then running to touch a green cushion.
setup.caption: 2. Hold up the two that make the colour. Then run and touch it.

flow.do: 1. Your child colours the three cards. 2. Clear a space to run.
flow.say: I will call a colour. Hold up the two cards that make it. Then run and touch something that colour.
flow.kid: Listen for the colour. Hold up two cards. Then run!

flow.do: Call green, orange and purple, in any order, a few times each.
flow.say: Orange! Which two cards make orange? Now run and touch something orange.
flow.kid: Hold up the two cards. Run and touch the colour.

ask.q: Why did you hold up red and yellow for orange?
good: Because red and yellow make orange.
We mixed them in the test.

flow.do: Your child is the caller, and you run.
flow.say: Now you call a colour, and I will run.
flow.kid: Now you call a colour. A grown-up runs.

check.q: The caller says 'Purple!' Which two cards do you hold up?
check.why: Red and blue make purple. Yellow and blue make green, and red and yellow make orange.

projects.title: My Colour Book: one mixed colour a day
projects.context: In this project you make a small book. Each day you mix one new colour, paint it on a page, and find things at home that have that colour.

materials.item: 3 sheets of paper, folded in half and tied with thread into a little book
red, yellow and blue paint, and a brush
crayons

schedule.what: Make the book. Mix orange and fill the orange page.
Mix green and fill the green page.
Mix purple and fill the purple page.

projects.record: The finished book, with a colour sum and things of that colour on every page.

setup.art: Three sheets of paper folded and tied with thread into a little book, with 'My Colour Book' on the cover.
setup.caption: 1. Fold and tie three sheets into a book.

setup.art: An open page with a painted red blob plus a yellow blob equals an orange blob, and crayon drawings of a carrot and a marigold below.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, paint one colour sum and draw things of that colour.

flow.do: 1. Make the book. 2. Your child mixes red and yellow and paints the colour sum on the first page. 3. They draw two orange things from home.
flow.say: Today's colour is orange. Mix red and yellow, and paint the sum. Then find two orange things at home and draw them.
flow.kid: Mix red and yellow. Paint the sum. Draw two orange things.

flow.do: Your child mixes yellow and blue for the green page, and draws two green things.
flow.say: Today's colour is green. Mix it, paint the sum, and draw two green things you can find.
flow.kid: Mix green. Paint the sum. Draw two green things.

flow.do: Your child mixes red and blue for the purple page, and draws two purple things. Then read the whole book together.
flow.say: Today's colour is purple. Mix it and paint the sum. Which page was easiest to fill? Why?
flow.kid: Mix purple. Paint the sum. Which page was easiest?

check.q: Which two paints did you mix for the purple page?
check.why: Red and blue make purple. You found purple things, like a brinjal or jamun.

challenges.title: Match the Leaf
challenges.context: This is a mixing challenge. You try to mix a green that matches a real leaf, using only red, yellow and blue paint.
challenges.problem: You want to paint a curry leaf so that it looks real. You have no green paint. Can you mix a green that matches a real leaf?
constraints: Use only red, yellow and blue paint, and water.
Paint a patch right next to the real leaf, to compare.
materials: a brush and a tumbler of water
a real leaf: a curry leaf, a coriander leaf or a leaf from a potted plant
general: Painters mix yellow and blue to make green.
More yellow makes a lighter green. More blue makes a darker green.
A tiny touch of red makes a bright green duller, like an older leaf.
creative: On another day, paint blue first, let it dry, then paint yellow on top, the way Kalamkari painters in Andhra Pradesh do.
Add water to make a pale green for the new leaves at the tip.
Paint the leaf with two greens: a darker one in the middle and a lighter one at the edges.
challenges.your_turn: Mix two greens and paint them next to the leaf. Which one matches best? What did you add to make it match?

setup.art: A real curry leaf lying on white paper next to three painted green patches, light, middle and dark.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the leaf on paper. Paint green patches next to it.

setup.art: A child holding the leaf up beside a painted patch to compare, with a plate of mixed greens nearby.
setup.caption: 2. Compare. Which green matches best?

flow.do: Read the problem to your child, and put the leaf on the paper.
flow.say: We have no green paint. How can we make a green that looks like this leaf?
flow.kid: We have no green. How can we make one like this leaf?

good: Like in the Colour Mixing Test.

flow.do: Your child mixes greens and paints patches beside the leaf.
flow.say: Mix a green and paint a patch next to the leaf. Is it too light or too dark? What could you add?
flow.kid: Paint a patch next to the leaf. Too light or too dark?
flow.parent: Most leaves are a duller green than yellow and blue make. A very small touch of red helps. Let your child find this by trying.

flow.do: Your child picks the best patch and says why.
flow.say: Which green matches best? What did you add to make it match?
flow.kid: Which green matches best? What did you add?

check.q: Your green is too light. What could you add?
check.why: More blue makes the green darker. Water and more yellow would make it lighter still.

items.p: Draw a line from each colour sum to the colour it makes.
items.why: These are the three mixes from the Colour Mixing Test. A strong answer matches all three, and the child can say which paints they used.
items.art: Three colour sums on the left, each two coloured blobs with a plus sign, and three coloured blobs on the right: green, orange and purple.

items.p: Draw a plate with red, yellow and blue paint. Show two of the paints mixing, and the new colour they make in the middle. Colour it in.
items.a: A plate with red, yellow and blue blobs, and a green, orange or purple patch where two met.
items.why: A strong drawing shows two paints going in and a new colour coming out.
items.art: A blank round plate shape for the child to draw on.

items.p: Farhan, a boy in Class 1, mixes red, yellow and blue paint all together. What colour does he get?
items.why: Every paint soaks up some light. All three together soak up most of it, so very little light comes back. That is why the mix is dark brown, not bright or white.

items.p: Some colours come straight from the paint box. Others you mix. Put each colour in the right box: from the box, or mixed.
items.why: Red, yellow and blue are the primary colours, and the other paints cannot make them. Green, orange and purple are each mixed from two of them.

items.p: Kalamkari painters make green by painting yellow over blue.
items.why: True. Painters in Srikalahasti paint yellow over indigo blue, and the two colours together look green, as in Lakshmi's story.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: what happened when you tried to get yellow back out of green?
items.a: I added more yellow, but it only turned yellowish green. It never turned plain yellow.
items.why: A strong answer says what the child saw, and that the blue was still in the mix.

items.p: Three of these can be mixed from other paints. Which one cannot?
items.why: Yellow is a primary colour. Green, orange and purple can each be mixed from two primary colours.

items.p: Thenmozhi and her friend Anjali are mixing paints in Chennai.

views.says: If I mix every colour, I will get the most beautiful colour of all, a rainbow colour.
If I mix every colour, I will get a dark, muddy colour. Each paint makes the mix darker.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it down. Then say one thing the other girl has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks Anjali and uses the test: all three paints made dark brown. It also says Thenmozhi has something right: each paint alone is bright, and brown is a useful colour, for a tree trunk or soil.
items.why: Anjali is right about paint. Thenmozhi's guess is a common one. Mixing light works differently, which a later unit shows. Both girls are thinking about what mixing does.

items.p: Draw a green parrot. Then colour the two paints you would mix to paint them.
items.a: A green parrot, with a yellow blob and a blue blob beside the parrot.
items.why: A strong drawing shows green made from yellow and blue. Real parrot feathers are yellow and blue together too, as in the story.
items.art: A blank box with space for a parrot and two small circles for the paints.

items.p: Draw a bee flying to a bright flower. Colour the flower.
items.a: A bee near a brightly coloured flower.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a bright flower and a bee coming to the flower, because bright colours call bees and butterflies to their nectar.
items.art: A blank box with space for a flower and a bee.

items.p: Put the Drop by Drop test in order.
items: Add blue, one drop at a time
a: Add blue, one drop at a time
items.why: First we make yellow water, then we add blue to make green, then we try to undo the green with water.

items.p: Bornali, a girl in Class 1, adds 1 drop of blue to yellow water, and then 5 more drops. What happens to the green?
items.why: Each drop of blue adds more blue, which absorbs more light. So the green gets darker.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why did the green water stay green, even after you poured in lots of water?
items.a: The water spread the colours out, so it got paler. But the yellow and blue were both still there, so it was still green.
items.why: A strong answer says that the water made the colour paler but did not take out the blue or the yellow.

items.p: Here are four things. Say which two paints you would mix to paint each one, and a grown-up writes it.
items.why: A strong answer names the right mix for each. The tree trunk is brown, which needs all three.
items.art: A carrot, a brinjal, a banana leaf and a tree trunk in a row, with an empty label under each.

items.p: In a dark room, a red tomato still looks red.
items.why: False. We need light to see colours. With no light falling on the tomato, it cannot send red light to our eyes, so it looks black.

items.p: In the Colour Mixing Test, a girl mixed three colour sums with two paints each, and one with all three paints. How many new colours did she make?
items.why: Green, orange and purple make 3. The brown from all three makes 4.

items.p: Ask a grown-up to help you write the missing word. Paint ___ some of the light that falls on it, and sends the rest back to our eyes.
items.why: To absorb is to soak up. The light that is not absorbed comes back to us, and that is the colour we see.

items.p: Draw a torch shining on yellow paint and on brown paint. Draw more arrows of light coming back from the one that sends back more light.
items.a: More arrows coming back from the yellow paint, and very few from the brown.
items.why: Brown is a mix of all three paints, so it absorbs the most light. Yellow absorbs only a little, so lots of light comes back.
items.art: A torch on the left and two paint patches on the right, one yellow and one brown, with space to draw arrows.

items.p: A pigeon's neck shines green and then purple as they turn their head. What makes those colours?
items.why: Tiny layers in the feathers send back different colours as the pigeon moves. That is why the colour changes when they turn.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: green was not in the yellow pot or the blue pot. So where did the green come from?
items.a: Yellow paint soaks up blue light and blue paint soaks up red and yellow light. Together, green is what is left to come back to my eyes.
items.why: A strong answer says that each paint soaks up some light, and green is the light left over. Any answer that uses what the child saw in the test is good thinking.

quiz.p: You mix yellow and blue paint. What colour do you get?
quiz.why: Yellow and blue make green. Red and yellow make orange, and red and blue make purple.

quiz.p: You mix red and yellow paint. What colour do you get?
quiz.why: Red and yellow make orange, like a marigold or a carrot.
Red and blue make purple, like a brinjal or a jamun.

quiz.p: What are red, yellow and blue called in a paint box?
quiz.why: They are the primary colours. You cannot mix them from the other paints in the box, but you can mix many colours from them.

quiz.p: Which of these colours can you mix from two other paints?
quiz.why: Orange is mixed from red and yellow. Red and yellow are primary colours.

quiz.p: Is a mix of yellow and blue paint lighter or darker than the yellow?
quiz.why: The blue paint absorbs more of the light, so less light comes back. The green is darker than the yellow.

quiz.p: A girl adds lots of water to her green paint. What happens?
quiz.why: Water spreads the colours out, so the green gets paler. The yellow and blue are both still there.

quiz.p: What does paint do with some of the light that falls on it?
opts: It absorbs, or soaks up, the light
It stores the light for night
quiz.why: Paint absorbs some light and sends the rest back to our eyes. That is the colour we see.

quiz.p: Why do many flowers have bright colours?
quiz.why: Bright colours help bees and butterflies find a flower's nectar.

quiz.p: Why do we see a leaf as green?
opts: The leaf sends green light back to our eyes
The leaf makes green light in the dark
quiz.why: A leaf soaks up some of the light that falls on it and sends green light back to our eyes. With no light, there is no green to see.

applications: Painters mix a few paints to get the exact colour they need, instead of buying hundreds of pots.
A colour printer mixes yellow, magenta and cyan ink, with black, to print every colour in a photo.
Kalamkari painters in Andhra Pradesh paint yellow over indigo blue to make green.
Rangoli and kolam makers mix coloured powders for festivals like Pongal and Diwali.
Wall paint shops mix a little of a few strong colours into white paint to make any shade a family wants.

open_questions.q: How many colours can a person tell apart?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists often say about a million, but they do not agree on one number. It depends on how you count, and on who is looking.

open_questions.q: Why do we like some colours more than others?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies find that many people like blue. Others find that it depends on where you grew up and what you remember. Scientists still argue about it.

open_questions.q: What does a red flower look like to a bee?
open_questions.why_open: Bees see ultraviolet light but see red poorly. We can measure what light a bee's eyes take in. But nobody knows what the colours look like to the bee themself.

open_questions.q: Why are blue flowers and blue animals so rare?
open_questions.why_open: Many blue animals make their blue with tiny shapes, not pigment. Scientists think blue pigment may be hard for living beings to make, but nobody is sure.

ask_kids: What two paints would you mix to make the colour of your shirt?
What is the brightest colour in this room? What is the darkest?
Can you find something orange in the kitchen?
If you mixed the colours of your dinner, what colour would you get?
Is the sky the same blue in the morning and the evening?
Which colour would you invent, if you could make a new one?

jokes.j: Why did the yellow paint and the blue paint get married?
What did the red paint say to the yellow paint?
Why did the paintbrush go to the doctor?
jokes.a: It was feeling a bit off-colour!

jokes.j: What is purple and 5000 miles long?
Why did the purple paint call the red paint and the blue paint?
jokes.a: To say thank you, Amma and Appa!

jokes.j: Why was the white paint scared of the black paint?
jokes.a: It did not want to go grey!

jokes.j: What is red and smells like blue paint?
What is green and goes up and down?

maths.problem: A girl has 3 primary colours: red, yellow and blue. She mixes them two at a time. Red and yellow is one mix. How many different mixes of two can she make?
maths.answer: 3 mixes: red and yellow, red and blue, yellow and blue.
maths.explain: Take each pair once. Red goes with yellow and with blue, which is 2. Then yellow goes with blue, which is 1 more. 2 and 1 make 3.
maths.context: This is about the Colour Mixing Test, where you mixed two paints at a time.
maths.why_maths: Counting the pairs carefully tells you how many mixes to try, so none is missed.

maths.problem: In the Drop by Drop test, a girl's water was light green after 1 drop of blue and dark green after 6 drops. How many more drops made it dark?
maths.explain: Count on from 1 to 6: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. That is 5 more drops. More blue made the green darker.
maths.context: This is about the Drop by Drop test, where you added blue to yellow water one drop at a time.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two numbers shows how many drops it took to change light green into dark green.

maths.problem: A girl counts things in her kitchen: 3 green things, 1 purple thing and 4 red things. Make a tally. Which colour did she find most? Which was hardest to find?
maths.answer: Red, with 4, was found most. Purple, with 1, was hardest to find.
maths.explain: Draw one stroke for each thing: green has 3, purple has 1, red has 4. 4 is the biggest, and 1 is the smallest.
maths.context: This is about the Colour Hunt, where you looked for colours at home. Count the things in your own kitchen the same way.
maths.why_maths: A tally shows at a glance which colours are common at home and which are rare.

warmup.q: What do yellow and blue paint make?
What do red and yellow paint make?
What do red and blue paint make?
Name the three primary colours of a paint box.
What do all three paints make together?
Can you see colours in the dark?
warmup.a: No. We need light to see colours.

warmup.q: What colours are inside a green parrot's feathers?

roots.context: We have mixed paints and watched new colours appear. Now we ask what the green on the plate tells us about colour, about light, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Yellow and blue paint made green, and all three paints together made dark brown. Each paint soaks up some of the light that falls on it. Two paints soak up more than one, so less light comes back. So mixing paints makes each new colour by taking light away.
deep_truth.habit: We think mixing is adding: put more colours in, get more colour out. The test shows paint works the other way. Every paint you add takes away more light, so the mix gets darker.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Colour Mixing Test, every mix was darker than yellow, and red, yellow and blue together made dark brown. In Drop by Drop, each drop of blue made the green darker, and water only made it paler.

three.who_am_i: You see colours because light comes into your eyes. The green you saw was the light the paints left for you.
three.what_is_life: Living beings make their own colours. A flower's colours call bees, and a parrot's green is yellow and blue together.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of colours, and almost all of them begin with light from the Sun or a lamp. Each thing sends back its own part of that light.

roots.thread: Red, yellow and blue gave you orange, green, purple and many browns. All of those colours came from three pots and one light. Every colour you see is the same light, with a different part soaked up. Everything is conscious, and every paint, flower and feather meets the light in its own way.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, The Heart of Understanding (1988)
teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper, and you can see a cloud in it. Without the cloud there is no rain, without rain no tree, and without the tree no paper.
teachings.link: Look deeply at the green on your plate, and you can see the yellow and the blue in it. Without either one, there would be no green.

teachings.source: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Theory of Colours (1810)
teachings.teaching: Colours are the deeds and sufferings of light.
teachings.link: Paint takes some of the light away and sends the rest back. The colour you see is what happens when light meets the paint.

science.text: Paint mixing works by absorbing light: each paint soaks up some colours, and a mix soaks up more. Mixing coloured lights works the other way, by adding light.
How the eye and brain turn light into the feeling of green is still not understood.

other_view.view: Colour is not in the paint at all, only in the eyes and brain of whoever looks. The paint only soaks up and sends back light, and the green is made inside you. For many of them, the paint itself senses nothing.

practice.title: Watch one drop
practice.say: Put a glass of yellow water in front of you. Sit still and breathe slowly. Now let one drop of blue fall in, and don't stir. Watch it spread. Breathe in as it curls. Breathe out as it grows. Watch the green slowly fill the glass.
practice.kid: Sit still. Let one drop of blue fall in. Don't stir. Breathe slowly. Watch the green spread.

ask: Where was the green before you mixed the yellow and the blue?
If the room went dark, would the green still be there?
Is the colour in the paint, in the light, or in you?
roots.art: A child sitting very still before a glass of yellow water, watching a single drop of blue curl down through it and turn it green.

how_we_found_out.story: For hundreds of years, painters knew that yellow and blue paint make green. In 1805, the English painter Mary Gartside wrote a book about colour, with pictures made from patches of mixed watercolour. Many people thought that colours always mix the same way. So yellow light and blue light should make green too. In 1852, the German scientist Hermann von Helmholtz tested this. He took yellow light and blue light from a prism and made them fall on the same spot. The spot did not turn green. It looked nearly white. So why does paint make green? Helmholtz explained that each paint absorbs some of the light that falls on it. Yellow paint absorbs blue light. Blue paint absorbs red and yellow light. Mixed together, they absorb almost everything except green. So the green we see is the light that is left over. Mixing lights adds colours together. Mixing paints takes colours away.
how_we_found_out.who: Mary Gartside, an English painter; Hermann von Helmholtz, a German scientist
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Colours always mix the same way, so yellow light and blue light make green, like paint. Helmholtz mixed yellow and blue light and got nearly white, and explained that paint makes green by absorbing light.

founder: ideas/by_topic/light-seeing-and-shadows.md, Mixing Paints vs Lights: mix paints of primary colours to show subtractive results; mixing food colours in water.

ideas/by_topic/light-seeing-and-shadows.md, Theory of Colours: make natural dyes from plants and compare shades; a journal of colours noticed in a day; the 'colour tag' game where players merge to make new colours.
science: Subtractive colour mixing: pigments absorb parts of the spectrum, and a mixture absorbs what each absorbs, so it reflects less light.
Hermann von Helmholtz, 1852, on the theory of compound colours: spectral yellow and blue light mix to near white, unlike yellow and blue pigments.
Mary Gartside, An Essay on Light and Shade, on Colours, and on Composition in General, London, 1805.
Bees see ultraviolet and are poor at seeing red; many flowers have ultraviolet nectar guides.
Pigeon neck iridescence comes from thin-film structures in the feather barbules.
Green parrot feathers combine yellow psittacofulvin pigments with structural blue; blue mutant budgerigars lack the yellow.
C. V. Raman, 1922, The molecular scattering of light in water and the colour of the sea, after his 1921 voyage.
Kalamkari of Srikalahasti, Andhra Pradesh: hand-drawn with a bamboo kalam and natural dyes; green made by applying yellow over indigo.

playtest: Walked through every experiment, activity, game, project and challenge as a parent and a six-year-old in a city flat, and checked the minutes, the checks and the printables against the steps. Replaced the Colour Hunt check, which asked a pointless question, with one that matches its step. Made the colour-card game print six cards so two players have a set each, gave it a clear end, and listed the players. Cut the ultraviolet and sea-colour sentences and the printers box from the explanations, since they were too much for age 6 and repeated elsewhere. Replaced repeated unmixing, flower and dark-room questions, a weak joke and a marigold question that said "their" for one flower. Made the second-day Kalamkari idea optional, since blue paint needs time to dry. Left the three video slots unfilled, since no clip has been opened and checked.
